articles.title: Harris keeps 2028 door open as she hits midterm campaign trail, warns ‘28 won’t matter’ without 2026
articles.summary: Kamala Harris told Detroit voters she has not decided on a 2028 presidential run, stressing that the 2026 midterm elections must come first.
articles.body: Former Vice President Kamala Harris said Tuesday that she has not decided whether she will run for president again in 2028, telling voters in Detroit that the upcoming midterm elections must come first. Harris was directly asked during a fireside chat whether she had thought about running for president in 2028 and whether another White House campaign was "on your plate." "I have not decided if I'm going to run again," Harris said before turning the focus to the midterms. "I do, I do sincerely believe 28 won't matter if we don't get through 26." GAVIN NEWSOM SAYS HE WON'T RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 IF KAMALA HARRIS RUNS Harris said she was focused on traveling the country and reminding voters of the power of their voices ahead of the 2026 elections. "And I'm a big believer that you can be. When you focus on the thing out there, you trip on the thing over here." The exchange came during Harris' second event Tuesday in Detroit, where she participated in a fireside chat moderated by Rev. Dr. Wendell Anthony, president of the Detroit Branch NAACP and pastor of Fellowship Chapel, and Rev. Dr. Genetta Y. Hatcher, pastor of The Room Church. Before asking Harris about a possible 2028 campaign, Anthony encouraged those in attendance to vote and referenced early and mail-in voting. Harris was later presented with "take your souls to the polls" merchandise. KAMALA HARRIS CLAIMS GOP 'CHEATING' AHEAD OF MIDTERMS, SAYS SHE'S FOCUSED ON STOPPING THE 'MADNESS' Earlier Tuesday, Harris campaigned alongside Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed at a roundtable focused on Black maternal health and healthcare costs. Harris used the event to criticize President Donald Trump's healthcare policies and voice support for El-Sayed. Harris' remarks came as she focuses on the 2026 midterms while leaving open the possibility of another presidential campaign. Harris became the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024 after then-President Joe Biden ended his re-election campaign. Ted Cruz (Texas) on Tuesday criticized populist Republicans for proposing “right-wing socialism,” arguing the strategy will not pay off for the party. “I consider myself very much a populist, Cruz said on Fox News’s “The Will Cain Show,” claiming “the base that has elected me every time has been blue-collar workers.” “Here’s the…
articles.body:
GOP Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas) on Tuesday criticized populist Republicans for proposing “right-wing socialism,” arguing the strategy will not pay off for the party.

“I consider myself very much a populist, Cruz said on Fox News’s “The Will Cain Show,” claiming “the base that has elected me every time has been blue-collar workers.”

“Here’s the difference: the way to be a populist is not get in the [Sen.] Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) game of giving away free stuff,” the Texas senator told host Will Cain. “The way to be a populist is fight for the jobs of working men and women, fight for small businesses.”

Earlier this month, President Trump proposed to send every American adult a $5,000 dividend if Republicans hold on to control of Congress in November. But multiple GOP lawmakers, including senators , have criticized the proposal, noting it would add to the $40-plus trillion national debt .

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), on the other hand, has said he will prepare legislation to send those dividends to roughly 270 million Americans should the GOP hold serve in the House and Senate. If the federal government sends a check to every adult, the initiative’s price tag will exceed $1 trillion.

Cruz on Tuesday criticized Democrats for the crop of democratic socialists winning primaries across the country, and urged Republicans to avoid following their lead.

“There are two answers to ‘right-wing socialism’: no, and hell no,” Cruz wrote on social platform X , arguing that socialism “has been a train wreck” everywhere it has been implemented.

“There are misguided voices in MAGA saying, ‘Let’s embrace socialism lite,’” the former presidential candidate told Cain. “You know what? If we campaign and say, ‘We’ll be just like the Democrats except not as a generous Santa Claus,’ that’s a path to losing.”

articles.title: Wicker blasts Xi ahead of summit with Trump in DC
articles.summary: GOP Sen. Roger Wicker (Miss.) slammed Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday, ahead of the Asian leader’s summit with President Trump in Washington, D.C. During remarks on the Senate floor, Wicker said that had the White House asked him for “advice,” he would have suggested President Trump “not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such…
articles.body:
GOP Sen. Roger Wicker (Miss.) slammed Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday, ahead of the Asian leader’s summit with President Trump in Washington, D.C.

During remarks on the Senate floor, Wicker said that had the White House asked him for “advice,” he would have suggested President Trump “not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome.”

The Senate Armed Services Committee chair cited his “troubling issues” with Xi and the Chinese Communist Party for why he would not have invited the Chinese leader.

Trump is set to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday. The U.S. president and first lady Melania Trump will also host Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, for a state dinner at the White House the next day.

The summit, the two leaders’ first in-person meeting since May, will come as the two countries battle each other for dominance in the artificial intelligence race — and as lawmakers stateside warn about the risks the technology presents.

The meeting also will take place less than two months before a U.S.-China trade truce expires on Nov. 10. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Monday on CNBC’s “Squawk Box” that the two sides are considering lowering tariffs on “noncritical” products .

But Wicker also urged the president to raise other topics with Xi during the summit, including China’s support for Iran, its subjugation of Uyghur Muslims and persecution of Tibetan Buddhists, Christians and those practicing Falun Gong.

“For nearly a decade, President Xi has consigned more than a million Uyghurs to concentration camps in China’s Xinjiang region,” Wicker remarked. “I hope our president will take this visit as an opportunity to advocate for the Uyghur people.

“The fact that they remain in prison by the millions is a grave injustice and a reminder of Xi Jinping’s many human rights abuses.”

Wicker later said, “I know the president intends to discuss trade and artificial intelligence with the Chinese leadership, and rightfully so. Perhaps some progress will be made.”

But the Mississippi Republican also noted that Trump “should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator.”

articles.title: Chris Mason: From inside the room, how Burnham survived first Trump meeting
articles.summary: Burnham seemed nervous at first, knowing how explosive these encounters with Trump can be, writes BBC political editor Chris Mason.
articles.body:
As I crouched between the cameras, determined to catch Donald Trump's eye and ask a question, I listened to a president seeking to be magnanimous.

Remember, Trump can and does do warmth when he wants to, as well as acerbic.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, a mayor a matter of months ago, sat next to the most powerful man in the world.

Put like that, it sounds believable when he said in advance he was looking forward to the meeting, but there must have been a jab of nerves too.

Burnham did look a little nervous as us reporters trooped into the room, but then, for the most part, the compliments flowed from the president.

The original plan was for journalists to be invited in at the beginning of the meeting, perhaps just minutes after the men had first met.

Instead, we were kept waiting while the private talks took place, which came with the upside that they had more to say about each other and what they had discussed than would otherwise have been the case.

Burnham knew, the world knows, how explosive these rolling, free wheeling, live on camera encounters with Trump can go.

It is rollercoaster without a harness stuff.

Having got myself into the president's eyeline, I waited for the last syllable of Burnham's final word at the end of his opening remarks and I filled the brief silence with a question.

Was the prime minister a man you can do business with, I asked the president, given your political differences?

"I do, I think he's a natural business person. We've had a lot of discussions even before this meeting. We've spoken to each other numerous times on the phone. Yeah, I think so, I think so. He gets it. He understands what he has to do."

The warmth was self evident. Perhaps the Downing Street nerves will have eased a bit.

But how long would the questions keep going? This is the president's theatre and he decides how long the public performance lasts. On occasion they are way north of half an hour.

This was a meeting on neutral territory, a windowless, nondescript meeting room down a dingy corridor in the basement of the United Nations. This wasn't the Oval Office of the White House. Perhaps that dialled down the sense of occasion a notch.

Nonetheless, for how long could the president maintain the bonhomie and sense of agreement? A question about immigration, potentially a point of friction, came and went without incident. So too did the Burnham government's decision, announced by the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who was in the room, to sanction settlements in the West Bank, a decision which infuriated Israel.

But on the future of the Chagos islands, the president couldn't hide his view that Britain's decision to cede sovereignty of them to Mauritius and then rent back the military base on Diego Garcia was "terrible."

Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal

The president added: "I think the prime minister is going to be looking at [the deal]" and Burnham replied "yep".

Later, it was my turn to do a short interview with the prime minister on behalf of all of the broadcasters.

Burnham emphasised that the meeting was "very encouraging" and "we've established a good connection."

But what about the Chagos deal? Would it change, I asked. Pointedly, he described it as a deal he had "inherited".

"We've got to find a resolution, and so work will continue now…to see where that resolution might lead."

In other words, it looks like it is going to change.

Flashpoints down the track with Trump are near inevitable — barely any leader avoids them with this administration, and Burnham may want to lean into some, in time.

And even those he doesn't might lean into him, Chagos possibly one of them.

But outwardly Burnham has a relationship with the president he can now build on after this opening face to face conversation.

What followed in the prime minister's remaining meetings at the UN were diplomacy by convention, not the wild ride with Trump he had just stepped off and survived.

articles.title: Trump-backed Missouri congressional map returns to Supreme Court for third time
articles.summary: The fight over Missouri’s congressional map returned to the U.S. Supreme Court for a third time late Tuesday, after an appeals court ordered the revival of new districts backed by President Donald Trump.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The fight over Missouri’s congressional map returned to the U.S. Supreme Court for a third time late Tuesday, after an appeals court ordered the revival of new districts backed by President Donald Trump. The new map was drawn to help Republicans gain a U.S. House seat in the pivotal midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. The Supreme Court has twice blocked efforts to use it in November. The latest emergency appeal comes after an unusual federal appeals court ruling that ordered a last-minute return to a GOP-friendly map even after the Supreme Court halted such a move. The justices had left in place a Missouri Supreme Court decision requiring the state to use its previous map. The state court ruled that the new districts could not take effect unless voters approved them in a statewide referendum. The U.S. Supreme Court gave supporters of the new map until midday Wednesday to respond to the latest appeal. The dispute has caused confusion for over a million potential voters who could be shuffled among districts. Absentee voting already is underway in Missouri using districts adopted in 2022, after the last census. The new congressional map backed by Trump significantly reshapes a Kansas City-based district held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver. Republicans hope the map could help them win seven of the state’s eight House seats — one more than they currently hold. Missouri’s redistricting battle has been the longest and most complex among roughly a dozen states that sought to change their U.S. House districts over the past year. Districts are usually redrawn at the start of each decade, after a census. But Trump spurred a spate of mid-decade redistricting last year when he urged Republican-led states to redraw districts to gain an edge in the midterm.

articles.title: Florida AG accuses teacher of labeling student a 'misogynist' over 'conservative views': 'She should be fired'
articles.summary: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier alleges a Pine View School teacher bullied a conservative eighth grader and labeled him a "misogynist."
articles.body: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier alleged that a teacher harassed and attempted to "cancel" an eighth-grade student and labeled him a "misogynist" over what Uthmeier described as the student's conservative political views. Uthmeier sent a letter to Sarasota County Schools' Superintendent Terry Connor and the school board over allegations that a Pine View School history teacher, Liz Ballard, singled out the eighth grade student on multiple occasions over his political views. Ballard often brings up political topics during class despite the student telling her that his parents "expressly forbid" him from participating in the political discussions, according to the letter. The parents' demand was ignored and the teacher continued to hold political discussions, using the student as the "conservative perspective in the classroom," the attorney general said. WASHINGTON FATHER SUES SCHOOL DISTRICT FOR DENYING RELIGIOUS OPT-OUT FOR 5TH GRADER FROM LGBTQ INSTRUCTION The teacher even labeled the student a "misogynist," spread that characterization around the school and "openly questioned the suitability and influence of the student's father," Uthmeier said in the letter. Uthmeier's letter says multiple parents previously initiated HR investigations involving Ballard. If the bullying and harassment allegations are true, Uthmeier said the teacher would have violated Florida law, School Board policy and basic ethical principles for educators. "Ms. Ballard singled out this student and, in defiance of his parents' express instructions, pressured him to defend political positions on demand in front of his classmates," Uthmeier wrote. PORTLAND PARENT BANNED FROM SCHOOL EVENTS AFTER OPPOSING GENDER IDENTITY ASSIGNMENT FILES LAWSUIT "She made disparaging remarks about his father. And by facilitating the spread of a damaging label throughout the school, she engaged in the reputational destruction of a child. Ms. Ballard's deliberate bullying and harassment of this eighth-grade student violated Florida law, School Board policy, and at least six ethical principles," he continued. He said she should be dismissed from her role with the school district and her educator certificate should be revoked if the allegations turn out to be true. "If true, she should be fired and never teach in Florida again," he said. The attorney general gave the superintendent and school board an Oct. 1 deadline to update his office on the actions the district has taken or will take to address the allegations. Connor said Sarasota County Schools received a letter from Uthmeier about allegations involving teacher. "Every student deserves a classroom where they feel safe, respected, and free to learn. No student should face harassment, humiliation, or retaliation because of their beliefs or their family's views. Respect for students and parents is fundamental to the trust our community places in our schools." "The allegations in the letter warrant careful attention. We will examine the relevant facts and records, ensure a fair process for all involved, and take appropriate action based on the findings and requirements. To protect student privacy and the process's integrity, we will limit public discussion of individual details. This does not reduce our commitment to accountability. articles.title: White House to roll out the red carpet for historic Xi Jinping visit
articles.summary: Trump and Xi are expected to discuss a range of issues from trade to AI during the latter's multi-day visit to Washington.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump will host Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Washington, with everything from AI to trade and Taiwan on the agenda for the leaders of the global superpowers.

Xi is expected to be greeted personally by Trump at Andrews Air Force Base on Wednesday, followed by a White House welcoming ceremony on Thursday featuring a military flyover and nearly 500 military personnel.

The trip marks Xi's first state visit to the US in just under a decade and his third meeting with Trump since the US president began his second term in office.

Adding to the high-stakes state visit, a US-China trade agreement reached last year is set to expire in November.

The trade truce - reached in October 2025 as Trump and Xi met in South Korea - saw Washington suspend steep tariff increases on Chinese goods while Beijing eased back from restricting rare earth exports critical for manufacturing.

Experts said they will be watching for some sort of announcement around an extension of this agreement during the upcoming state visit.

Xi's trip to Washington, which ends on Friday, will have plenty of pomp and pageantry, and includes lavish dinners, private tours and performances.

David Sacks, a fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, described the planned extravagant welcome by Trump as "really unprecedented".

"From meeting Xi Jinping at Andrews Air Force Base to having a flyover for Xi as well, this is not something afforded to any US ally," Sacks said, "much less an adversary like China.

"It's quite, quite stunning," he continued.

Trump is expected to address several issues as he meets Xi, particularly on tariffs and trade.

The US president has long criticised his country's trade deficit with China, which stands at more than $91bn (£68.2bn), according to the latest US Census Bureau data .

Also, Chinese rare earth exports to the US are down despite the agreement last October.

US and Chinese officials held trade talks on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday but failed to make meaningful progress ahead of the Xi visit, multiple sources told the BBC.

The talks focused on finding areas of agreement around non-tariff trade issues and agricultural exports, according to sources familiar with White House thinking.

US negotiators are expected to continue talks with Chinese counterparts in Washington on Wednesday after Xi's arrival.

Rare look at the remote engine rooms powering China's AI ambitions

Another likely talking point between Trump and Xi is artificial intelligence, a topic that David Firestein from the Bush China Foundation said has "climbed rapidly toward the top of the agenda" ahead of this visit.

China and the US are competing in what has been described as an AI arms race. But after a series of recent high-profile security incidents involving the emergent technology, there has been growing pressure on the Trump administration to regulate AI and slow its development.

Senator Bernie Sanders wrote on X this week: "For the sake of all humanity, Trump and Xi must negotiate a treaty NOW to pause AI and ban superintelligence before it's too late."

Trump's former White House advisor Steve Bannon and some Republicans in Congress have also warned about dangers posed by AI.

The president, who views the technology as vital to the US economy and a battleground in a global struggle for power, has been reluctant.

He views defeating China in the AI race as a primary objective. "Whoever wins AI, wins," Trump has said.

Firestein told the BBC he expects Trump and Xi to discuss ways for AI collaboration.

On Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng and said the two had "very successful" talks on trade and AI.

Experts who spoke to BBC said any major breakthroughs on AI or other issues are unlikely to occur during the many Trump-Xi meetings planned this week.

Then there is Taiwan, which remains an ongoing diplomatic thorn.

The US Congress has approved a multibillion-dollar arms sale to Taiwan that awaits Trump's signature. He has held off for now, viewing the move as a bargaining chip with China.

China has long vowed to "reunify" with self-governing Taiwan and has not ruled out the use of force.

Firestein said he expects Xi will be looking for Trump to either commit to extending the delay of the arms sale or somehow avoiding the sale altogether.

Xi - like Trump - is also facing economic headwinds at home, and is expected to use this visit as an opportunity to discuss deepening US-China trade.

However, that presents a potential political problem for Trump. Some members of his cabinet and his supporters view China with deep suspicion.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy issued a letter to Ford Motor Company in September, urging the company to cut ties with China due to national security concerns and protection of American jobs.

Regardless of the clear hurdles that remain before any new US-China deals are inked, it is clear that Trump views personal contact with Xi as vital to the process.

"Trump has made a decision that no matter what, we need to not have a confrontational relationship with China," Stephen Orlins, president at the National Committee on US-China Relations, said.

"He believes that the more he and President Xi meet, the less confrontational that relationship will be," Orlins continued, "and he is right."

With additional reporting by Daniel Bush, Washington correspondent

articles.title: Trump administration accuses banned media outlets of 'falsehoods' ahead of court hearing
articles.summary: The US Justice Department's response to a lawsuit filed by CNN, Politico and MS NOW also cites national security.
articles.body:
The US Justice Department has filed documents that accuse three media outlets banned from the White House of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods" and reporting which "threatened national security" as it prepared to defend the move in court.

Last week, President Donald Trump barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news".

After their reporters had their passes confiscated and were denied access to the building, the three outlets jointly launched legal action , calling the move unconstitutional.

On Wednesday, a judge is set to decide whether to issue an order temporarily lifting the ban, pending a full hearing.

According to a court filing by the Justice Department in a District of Columbia court, the three outlets were issued with a list of "reporting incidents" by the White House ahead of the ban.

The filing cites a number of stories about construction at the White House - including about a security bunker and the building of a new ballroom, as well as a report on an internal information leak investigation.

It goes on to say that "access to the White House is a privilege, not a right".

The three media organisations have argued that the ban breaches their rights under the First Amendment, which forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press.

In a joint statement confirming legal action against the government, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.

"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

Major TV networks have withdrawn from a media-sharing arrangement of video and images of the president, known as the pool, in protest over the ban.

Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president.

articles.title: Mamdani fires back at Netanyahu, calls Israeli leader 'architect of horrific genocide' ahead of UN visit
articles.summary: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani fired back at Benjamin Netanyahu's accusations of supporting Hamas by citing the ICC arrest warrant for alleged war crimes.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani fired back at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday after the Israeli leader accused him of supporting Hamas terrorists and inciting unrest against Jewish New Yorkers, escalating their long-running feud days before Netanyahu is expected in the city. When asked by reporters about Netanyahu's video, Mamdani rejected the prime minister's accusations. "We all know that what the prime minister has said in that video is not true," Mamdani said. "What we do know to actually be the truth when it comes to the prime minister is that he is the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity." NETANYAHU ACCUSES MAMDANI OF 'FOMENTING HATE,' SAYS RHETORIC IS MAKING NEW YORK JEWS AFRAID The ICC issued the arrest warrant in November 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, but Netanyahu and the Israeli government have rejected the allegations and challenged the court's actions. Mamdani went further, leveling additional accusations against the Israeli leader days before he is slated to speak at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. "And as the prime minister, he is the architect of horrific genocide against Palestinians," Mamdani asserted. "And just a few days ago, his military killed an 11-year-old boy in what is deemed to be a safe zone in Gaza. So that is what I have to say to his video." ISRAELI UN ENVOY BLASTS MAMDANI AS 'CLOWN' OVER CALL TO ARREST NETANYAHU: 'IT'S A STUNT' The mayor was responding to comments Netanyahu made earlier Tuesday in a video pledging to "tell the truth" about Mamdani when he speaks at the U.N. "Shame on you, Mr. Mamdani. Shame on you for supporting the Hamas terrorist monsters who butchered our people. Shame on you for inciting riots against New York Jews," Netanyahu said in the video posted to X. "I'm coming to the U.N. I am going to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers, and I'm going to tell you the truth about you," he added. EXCLUSIVE: ISRAELI PRESIDENT HERZOG BLASTS MAMDANI, PRAISES TRUMP, SOUNDS ALARM ON IRAN The exchange is the latest chapter in an ongoing public feud between the two leaders and comes as Netanyahu prepares to visit the city Mamdani leads. Earlier this year, Mamdani explored whether New York City could execute the ICC warrant against Netanyahu — an issue he had campaigned on — before acknowledging that the city could not enforce the warrant on its own. Mamdani has previously called Netanyahu a "war criminal" and an "architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people." He also said over the summer that Netanyahu was "not welcome" in New York City. "I want to be equally clear: Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large," Mamdani said at the time. Mamdani has also defended New Yorkers' right to protest during Netanyahu's visit, though he has said he is not encouraging them to demonstrate. MAMDANI DODGES ON ‘POLITICAL THEATER’ OF EMPTY NETANYAHU ARREST THREAT, CALLS FOR US ACTION AND NYC PROTESTS When asked in July what New Yorkers frustrated with Netanyahu should do when the Israeli leader visited the city, Mamdani pointed to protest as an option. "One of the bedrocks of our city is protest," Mamdani said. "It is something that has been a part of what makes our city so special, that New Yorkers can express themselves whether they are in support or in opposition no matter on whatever topic." More recently, Mamdani clarified that he had no plans to participate in protests surrounding Netanyahu's visit and said he had not encouraged New Yorkers to demonstrate. "To New Yorkers, I have never encouraged them to protest," Mamdani said last week. "What I have always told them is that they have the right to do so in the city."
